name: Avellaneous
lede: Avellaneous is an old word for the light brown of a hazelnut, rare in speech but one of the commonest colors in the paintings of our archive.

sections.title: The color of a hazel nut
sections.body:
Paterson defines avellaneous as the light brown of the hazel-nut or filbert-nut [1]. The word sits among his entries of brown colors [1]. Ridgway's 1912 plate 40 gives it as a swatch (hue 17''', tone b), and the ISCC-NBS system placed it in block 57 [2]. On screen it is a tan with a pinkish cast, about six units from [[camel]] and near [[mushroom]], [[hazel]] and [[beige]] [2].

The books we hold say nothing else about it, so the word's history is undocumented here [1][2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a surprising number: in our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 1,847, nearly one in thirteen [3]. The top matches are not oil paintings but East Asian works on aged silk and paper, such as Kano Tan'yu's Bird on a Lotus Bud, where the color covers about 98 per cent [3]. The earliest is a funerary papyrus of about 1069 BC [3]. Most of this is the ground of aged silk, paper and canvas, so the match reflects supports as much as pigments [3].
